articles.title: Can China’s New Bridge Revive Trade With North Korea Despite UN Sanctions? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Can China’s New Bridge Revive Trade With North Korea Despite UN Sanctions?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
China and North Korea have opened a major new border bridge after more than a decade of delays, signalling closer economic ties between Beijing and Pyongyang as both countries seek to expand trade and improve cross-border connectivity.
Trucks carrying the national flags of both countries crossed the three-kilometre New Yalu River Bridge on Thursday, connecting the Chinese city of Dandong with North Korea. Although construction was completed in 2014, the bridge remained unused because North Korea had not finished the necessary approach roads and customs facilities.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang described the opening as the beginning of a new phase in bilateral relations, according to China’s official Xinhua news agency.
The bridge is expected to facilitate trade, improve customs procedures and strengthen economic cooperation in border areas. However, analysts caution that its opening does not necessarily signal an immediate return to the levels of trade that existed before international sanctions against North Korea were tightened.
China and North Korea Seek Closer Economic Ties
The opening represents the latest development in improving relations between Beijing and Pyongyang, following two summits between their leaders over the past year.
In his video address, Li said the bridge would strengthen economic and trade cooperation while encouraging greater exchanges between the two populations.
North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song also delivered a video address, although North Korean state media had not reported the event at the time of the announcement.
The new crossing could make it easier to transport heavy machinery, industrial raw materials and energy products into North Korea, supporting the country’s economic development plans.
China remains North Korea’s largest trading partner by a substantial margin, despite international sanctions imposed over Pyongyang’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes.
Chinese exports to North Korea reached $2.3 billion in 2025, a six-year high and a 25% increase from the previous year. However, trade remains below pre-2017 levels, when the United Nations strengthened sanctions against North Korea.
The bridge could help facilitate further growth, although the extent of its impact will depend on border procedures, trade restrictions and the willingness of both governments to expand commercial exchanges.
Why the Bridge Does Not Guarantee a Trade Boom
Despite the new infrastructure, a rapid return to unrestricted trade is unlikely.
United Nations sanctions have restricted a range of goods, economic activities and labour transfers involving North Korea in response to its weapons programmes. China and Russia, both permanent members of the UN Security Council, supported sanctions resolutions until 2017 but have since questioned the effectiveness and legitimacy of maintaining certain restrictions.
Analysts also suggest that Pyongyang remains cautious about becoming even more economically dependent on Beijing.
Lim Eul-chul of Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies said the bridge was unlikely to produce an immediate return to pre-sanctions trade levels.
Nevertheless, improved transport infrastructure could increase the efficiency of permitted commerce and make it easier for North Korea to obtain equipment and materials needed for domestic development.
The opening therefore represents an expansion of economic connectivity rather than proof that longstanding political and regulatory barriers have been removed.
Dandong Hopes for an Economic Revival
The bridge’s opening also carries significant implications for Dandong, the Chinese border city that has historically served as the principal gateway for trade with North Korea.
The city’s economy benefited from cross-border commerce during the early 2000s, but delays in opening the new bridge limited its potential to expand trade and attract investment.
Until Thursday, most cross-border goods had travelled through an older bridge approximately 10 kilometres upstream. Built 83 years ago, the existing crossing combines a railway track with a single-lane road and remains the busiest of roughly 15 crossing points along the countries’ 1,350-kilometre border.
The new bridge offers additional capacity and the potential to improve the movement of goods between the two countries.
Residents in Dandong welcomed the opening, expressing hopes that the new crossing would bring greater commercial activity and attract more visitors to the area.
However, the extent of any economic revival will depend on whether increased infrastructure capacity translates into sustained trade volumes, investment and employment.
Regional Implications for East Asian Security
The opening also comes amid closer strategic cooperation between China and North Korea, a relationship that carries implications for the wider region.
South Korea is monitoring whether the bridge will be followed by additional measures to strengthen ties between Beijing and Pyongyang. A South Korean Unification Ministry official described the opening as the first visible implementation of agreements reached during a summit between the countries’ leaders in June.
Seoul is particularly attentive to the possibility that closer economic relations could accompany broader strategic coordination between the two neighbours.
Meanwhile, North Korea has strengthened its relationship with Russia amid the war in Ukraine. The United States and South Korea have accused Moscow of providing sensitive military assistance to Pyongyang in exchange for North Korean support for Russia’s war effort.
Against this backdrop, stronger China-North Korea economic links could further complicate regional security calculations, although the bridge itself is primarily intended to facilitate trade and transport.
What Comes Next for China-North Korea Relations?
The New Yalu River Bridge provides Beijing and Pyongyang with new infrastructure for expanding economic cooperation after years of delays and pandemic-related disruption.
Its significance will ultimately depend on how extensively the two governments use the crossing, whether trade continues to grow and whether additional agreements translate into practical cooperation.
For China, stronger cross-border commerce could support economic activity in Dandong while reinforcing its position as North Korea’s principal economic partner. For Pyongyang, the bridge offers improved access to essential goods, industrial equipment and energy supplies.
However, international sanctions, North Korea’s concerns about economic dependence and broader regional security tensions will continue to constrain the relationship.
The opening is an important step towards closer economic ties, but whether it leads to a sustained trade boom will depend on decisions extending well beyond the construction of the bridge itself.
With information from Reuters.

articles.title: South Korea Chip Stocks Slide on AI Concerns - Markets.com
articles.summary: South Korea Chip Stocks Slide on AI Concerns  Markets.com
articles.full_text:
South Korean chip stocks dropped sharply on Thursday, October 15, as investors reassessed the earnings outlook for the artificial intelligence industry and the risks surrounding global semiconductor investment.
Intraday reports showed SK Hynix falling around 11%, while Samsung Electronics declined roughly 9%–10%. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi fell about 8% during the session. These figures represent reported intraday moves rather than confirmed closing prices.
The declines formed part of a wider retreat in Asian technology shares following weakness on Wall Street. For South Korea, the selling highlighted how closely market sentiment has become tied to the performance of its largest semiconductor businesses.
The central question is whether rapid AI infrastructure spending can sustain the growth in chip demand and profitability that investors have anticipated.
The selloff does not, by itself, establish that demand for AI chips has weakened. Share prices reflect expectations about future earnings, which can change before orders or revenue show a clear slowdown.
Investors must assess several moving parts: how much cloud providers will continue spending, whether those investments generate adequate returns, and how quickly chipmakers can increase production.
Strong demand can support rising sales while still leaving stocks vulnerable if valuations already assume exceptional growth. Higher interest rates can add pressure by reducing the present value investors assign to future profits and increasing financing costs across the AI investment chain.
Product differences also matter. High-bandwidth memory used alongside AI accelerators, conventional DRAM and NAND flash storage serve different functions. Their pricing and competitive conditions can diverge, making broad claims about a single “memory cycle” less useful than examining each business separately.
A separate development has brought export restrictions back into focus.
Reports citing people familiar with the discussions indicate that SK Hynix’s US subsidiary, Solidigm, is seeking permission to install additional American chipmaking equipment at the group’s Dalian facility in China. The reported proposal links that expansion to plans for a new NAND flash memory factory in the United States.
Additional Chinese production could help generate funding for the proposed US investment. However, the discussions remain unconfirmed by the companies, and the equipment request should not be treated as an approved expansion.
The situation illustrates the competing pressures facing multinational chipmakers. Washington wants additional semiconductor manufacturing investment in the United States while restricting equipment shipments that could expand Chinese production.
For investors, the implications depend on the eventual licensing terms, construction commitments and funding requirements. The reported negotiations do not establish that export restrictions caused Thursday’s share-price declines.
South Korea’s latest trade figures provide a stronger picture of current semiconductor demand than the stock-market performance alone suggests.
Official figures show September semiconductor exports reached $60.30 billion, up 262.8% from a year earlier. The government linked the increase to expanding export volumes and higher contract prices as memory demand continued to grow.
Those figures cover total semiconductor exports. They should not be presented as memory-only sales or substituted directly for the unverified $37.59 billion figure in the original brief.
The contrast between strong exports and falling shares is significant. Export data describe business already taking place, while equity prices incorporate expectations about future supply, margins and growth.
Investors can therefore acknowledge robust current trading conditions while becoming more cautious about how long unusually favourable conditions will last.
New factories could support higher shipment volumes and strengthen manufacturers’ competitive positions. They could also put pressure on pricing if production eventually grows faster than demand.
A potential supply increase around 2029 should be treated as a risk scenario rather than a confirmed turning point. Construction schedules, equipment installation, manufacturing yields and customer qualification will determine when planned capacity becomes commercially available.
The effect will also depend on the products being manufactured. Additional NAND capacity would not necessarily resolve shortages in advanced high-bandwidth memory.
For South Korea, dependence on a small number of major exporters creates another consideration: changes in semiconductor sentiment can have an outsized effect on the domestic equity market.
Upcoming company updates will help investors compare market concerns with actual business conditions. Important indicators include memory contract prices, order commitments, inventory levels, capital expenditure and expected returns from new facilities.
Developments in US equipment licensing could also influence the timing and cost of SK Hynix’s expansion plans.
South Korea’s chip selloff reflects growing uncertainty about future returns from the AI investment boom. Strong exports remain a source of support, but sustained confidence will depend on whether demand, pricing and cash generation can keep pace with expanding production and investment.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s China RAM Warning Raises Questions for Samsung, SK Hynix as South Korea Faces Potential Memory Chip Oversupply and Less Time To Diversify - TradingView
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s China RAM Warning Raises Questions for Samsung, SK Hynix as South Korea Faces Potential Memory Chip Oversupply and Less Time To Diversify  TradingView
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk warned that China will be “making a lot” of random-access memory (RAM) by 2028, amplifying concerns that a future chip glut could expose South Korea’s dependence on Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. SSNLF and SK Hynix Inc. SKHY.
Musk Flags China’s Growing Memory Chip Output
"China will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028," Musk wrote Thursday on X, responding to P Equity Research’s summary of a South Korean column. The column warned that new capacity could cause oversupply in 2029 and argued Korea has two to three years to develop alternative growth industries.
China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies, aka CXMT, said in September its fifth-generation DRAM platform had entered mass production. Reuters reported that the company says its process can produce at least 50% more gross chip dies per wafer than its predecessor, underscoring China’s growing manufacturing capabilities.
South Korea’s Chip Dependence Raises Economic Risks
Reuters reported that CXMT held about 7.7% of the global DRAM market in 2025. However, it trails Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron in high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. Musk previously acknowledged China’s manufacturing scale but said advanced memory "will be harder to solve."
South Korea’s government reported that September semiconductor exports jumped 263% to $60.3 billion, nearly half of its record $120.9 billion in total exports. Any future reversal in chip prices could therefore hit national export earnings.
Samsung And SK Hynix Face Market Uncertainty
Gartner expects memory to generate $837 billion, or 54% of worldwide semiconductor revenue, in 2026, up from 27% in 2025. It forecasts tight supplies through 2027. SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung told Reuters in July that demand could exceed supply beyond 2030.
Samsung shares fell 9.5% and SK Hynix lost 11.1% Thursday, Reuters reported, amid a wider technology selloff driven by U.S. inflation concerns and doubts over AI investment. The declines followed earlier market jitters over China’s chipmaking advances.

articles.summary: North Korea, China Open Border Bridge to Boost Trade  Tempo.co English
articles.full_text:
October 15, 2026 | 03:19 pm
TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - China and North Korea on Thursday officially opened their most significant land border crossing, aimed at rejuvenating trade and commerce after years of strained ties and disruptions.
A ceremony was held to launch the New Yalu River Bridge, Chinese state media Xinhua News reported.
Meanwhile, China News Service showed visuals of trucks adorned with the national flags of China and North Korea on the bridge, which itself was decorated in flags.
Spectators crowded on a road on the Chinese side, in Dandong city, overlooking the ceremony. In Sinuiju city on the North Korean side, work on the approaching road and compound remained unfinished.
'A new chapter'
The cable-stayed bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused until now due to lack of connecting roads on the North Korean side, South Korea's Yonhap News agency reported.
The opening was further delayed by the COVID pandemic which prompted North Korea to close its borders. Train journeys between the East Asian neighbors only restarted in March after six years, but Pyongyang is yet to resume issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, which once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.
The bridge's opening marks the latest sign of warning ties between Beijing and Pyongyang which have conducted two summits between their leaders in the past year.
"(Bilateral) relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter," Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in a video address at the opening, the official Xinhua news agency said.
He added that the border crossing would "strongly promote" economic and trade cooperation and strengthen exchanges between their people.
A conduit for trade
Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told the AFP news agency he expected hundreds of vehicles to cross every day.
"The bridge could become a conduit for China's abundant goods and resources to flow into North Korea and give its economy a significant boost," he said.
At the same time, experts believe North Korea remains cautious of greater dependence on China.
"The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade," said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies. But it will help move heavy equipment and raw material North Korea needs for development, he said.
China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner despite a series of UN sanctions banning the flow of goods and workers to North Korea over its missile and nuclear weapons program.

articles.summary: Trucks line up as long-delayed China-North Korea bridge officially opens  Japan Today
articles.full_text:
China and North Korea officially marked the long-delayed opening of their most significant land border crossing on Thursday, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of soured ties and pandemic-related disruptions to cross-border exchange.
The 3-km New Yalu River Bridge and the Chinese customs at the end of the 1.3-km crossing saw increased activity over the past few days, with trucks adorned with Chinese flags waiting on the bridge ahead of a crossing on Thursday.
Crowds also gathered on the Chinese side along a road overlooking the bridge.
Chinese and North Korean flags also lined the cable-stayed bridge with towering pylons that had been completed in 2014 but remained unused, while approach roads and a customs compound on the North Korea end remained unfinished.
On Thursday, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported the countries held an opening ceremony for the new bridge. North Korea's state media have yet to report on the scheduled event.
The opening signals progress in bilateral relations between Beijing and Pyongyang, marked by two summit meetings between their leaders in the past year.
China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner, even after a series of U.N. sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers to and from North Korea over the country's defiant missile and nuclear weapons development.
China and Russia, two U.N. Security Council permanent member states that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans.
Analysts said North Korea, despite the potential economic boost from active trade, remains cautious of greater dependence on China. Russia is accused by countries such as the US and South Korea of supplying sensitive military assistance to the North in return for Pyongyang's help in fighting the war in Ukraine.
"The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade," said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
But the bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products needed for North Korea's development projects, he said.
China's exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3 billion last year, a 25% increase over the previous year. That was still well below levels before U.N. sanctions were tightened in 2017.

articles.title: South Korea's ICT Exports Top $70 Billion for First Time as Semiconductors Approach 80% Share - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: South Korea's ICT Exports Top $70 Billion for First Time as Semiconductors Approach 80% Share  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Global artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investment has propelled South Korea's information and communications technology (ICT) exports past the $70 billion monthly threshold (approximately 93.8 trillion won) for the first time in history. Semiconductors led the charge, accounting for more than 80% of total ICT exports, while solid-state drive (SSD) exports for AI data centers surged by more than 500%.
According to the "September 2026 ICT Import/Export Trends" report released by South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT on the 14th, ICT exports last month reached $75.15 billion (approximately 100.7 trillion won), up 195.8% year-over-year. This figure exceeded the previous record of $59.98 billion (approximately 80.4 trillion won) set in August by $15.17 billion in just one month. Exports skipped the $60 billion range entirely and vaulted straight to the $70 billion milestone.
ICT exports had dipped from $57.28 billion in June to $53.35 billion in July, rebounded to $59.98 billion in August, and then exploded in September. ICT accounted for 62.1% of total industrial exports ($120.94 billion), marking the second consecutive month above 60% following August's 61.0% and sustaining an all-time high level.
Imports rose 55.3% year-over-year to $21.43 billion (approximately 28.7 trillion won), while the trade balance recorded a surplus of $53.71 billion (approximately 72 trillion won). The trade surplus also shattered August's $41.37 billion (approximately 55.5 trillion won), crossing the $50 billion threshold for the first time ever.
Semiconductors Drive Record-Breaking Growth
Semiconductors were at the center of the export record. September semiconductor exports surged 262.8% year-over-year to $60.33 billion (approximately 80.9 trillion won), setting a monthly record for the second consecutive month. Semiconductors accounted for 80.3% of total ICT exports.
Memory semiconductor exports were the primary growth engine, soaring 358.6% to $54.07 billion (approximately 72.5 trillion won). DRAM exports skyrocketed 552.2% to $33.26 billion (approximately 44.6 trillion won), while NAND Flash exports jumped 366.5% to $3.3 billion (approximately 4.4 trillion won). System semiconductor exports rose 28.9% to $5.49 billion (approximately 7.4 trillion won). Although foundry exports declined, the semiconductor back-end processing and fabless sectors lifted overall performance.
Rising memory prices also contributed to export growth. The fixed transaction price of 16Gb DRAM climbed steeply from $40 in June to $45 in July, $46.5 in August, and $48 in September. Over the same period, 128Gb NAND Flash prices rose from $28.8 to $30.6. The combination of increased demand for high-value memory products driven by AI infrastructure investment and rising general-purpose memory prices led to a simultaneous surge in export values.
Expanding AI data center investment also directly benefited computer and peripheral device exports. September computer and peripheral device exports surged 393% year-over-year to $7.16 billion (approximately 9.6 trillion won). Within this category, SSD exports skyrocketed 532% to $6.77 billion (approximately 9.1 trillion won), accounting for approximately 94.6% of total computer and peripheral exports. This was the result of explosive demand growth for high-capacity SSDs used in AI servers.
Mobile phone exports rose 28.2% to $1.9 billion (approximately 2.5 trillion won). This was driven by expanded sales of premium smartphone finished products, along with increased exports of components such as camera modules ($1.13 billion, up 32.5%) and 3D sensing modules.
In contrast, display exports fell 11.5% to $1.7 billion (approximately 2.3 trillion won). Demand for mobile organic light-emitting diode (OLED) panels declined as major smartphone launch schedules were adjusted, while downward pricing pressure from customers persisted. Telecommunications equipment exports also decreased 2.3% to $220 million (approximately 290 billion won), due to reduced exports of navigation equipment to Poland and Türkiye and wireless communication devices to Japan.
Regional Growth Led by the United States and China
By region, the U.S. market showed the steepest growth. September ICT exports to the United States surged 420.1% year-over-year to $15.17 billion (approximately 20.3 trillion won). Semiconductor exports to the U.S. jumped 700.1% to $10.32 billion (approximately 13.8 trillion won), while computer and peripheral device exports soared 654.7% to $3.59 billion (approximately 4.8 trillion won).
ICT exports to China (including Hong Kong), the largest export market, rose 228.9% to $30.4 billion (approximately 40.7 trillion won). The main driver was a 290.7% increase in semiconductor exports to China, which reached $26.63 billion (approximately 35.7 trillion won).
Elsewhere, exports to Taiwan rose 110.9% to $9.06 billion (approximately 12.1 trillion won), Vietnam increased 66.8% to $6.77 billion (approximately 9.1 trillion won), the European Union (EU) grew 128.5% to $2.96 billion (approximately 4 trillion won), India climbed 104.3% to $1.02 billion (approximately 1.4 trillion won), and Japan advanced 119.6% to $840 million (approximately 1.1 trillion won). Broad-based growth was evident across major export markets.
Gap Between Large Corporations and SMEs
Despite the overall ICT export boom, small and mid-sized enterprises (SMEs) grew at a relatively slower pace. SME ICT exports in September rose just 21.7% year-over-year to $6.65 billion (approximately 8.9 trillion won)—a markedly lower rate compared to the overall ICT export growth of 195.8%.
Looking at small enterprises alone, exports increased 17.3% to $1.93 billion (approximately 2.6 trillion won). Semiconductor exports (up 52.1%) and mobile phone exports (up 33.6%) increased, but computer and peripheral device exports declined 0.8%. The benefits of expanding AI data center investment have clearly been concentrated among large corporations.
On the import side, September ICT imports saw semiconductors rise 94.5% to $12.62 billion (approximately 16.9 trillion won), computer and peripheral devices increase 48.4% to $2.22 billion (approximately 3 trillion won), and mobile phones grow 40.9% to $1.67 billion (approximately 2.2 trillion won). By product category, semiconductors posted a trade surplus of $47.71 billion (approximately 64 trillion won), accounting for the majority of the total ICT trade surplus, while computer and peripheral devices also recorded a surplus of $4.94 billion (approximately 6.6 trillion won). Telecommunications equipment, however, posted a deficit of $200 million (approximately 270 billion won).

articles.title: Strengthening America’s AI Chip Export Controls - American Compass
articles.summary: Strengthening America’s AI Chip Export Controls  American Compass
articles.full_text:
How should federal law remedy the weaknesses in America’s export control regime for advanced AI chips?
Recommended Reading
Executive Summary
- The United States currently dominates global AI. America and its partners control the design and manufacture of advanced AI chips, as well as the production of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Export controls on chips and equipment have played an important role in maintaining this lead.
- This lead is not inevitable. The Chinese Communist Party in particular is aggressively seeking to catch up, and is exploiting serious vulnerabilities in the current American export control regime.
- Congress should close these gaps by mandating the use of location verification technology to combat illegal smuggling, ensuring partners’ export controls are aligned with American controls, codifying existing restrictions into law, and guaranteeing that no chip sales to adversaries harm American national security or constrain supply for American industry.
The Policy Question
The United States and its partners hold a commanding lead over China in the design and manufacture of advanced AI semiconductors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment (SME). The U.S. has placed restrictions on the sale and export of such chips and equipment to China and other adversaries, which has helped maintain that lead. But that export control regime has been subject to vacillating approaches by the executive branch and suffers from structural weaknesses that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is aggressively exploiting.
How should federal law remedy the weaknesses in America’s export control regime for advanced AI chips?
Why It Matters
Global AI leadership is an economic and national security imperative for the United States and its allies. The U.S. is currently the global leader in AI, due in large part to American and allied control of the most advanced AI chip design and manufacture. But this dominance is not guaranteed—with sufficient compute, China would be able to catch up and even overtake the U.S.
The CCP is committed to catching up and is ruthlessly exploiting structural deficits in American export controls to gain the chips and SME it needs to do so. This represents a serious vulnerability to American economic and national security.
State of Play
The United States and its partners dominate the supply chain for advanced AI semiconductors.

This control over the AI chip stack, from tools to design to manufacture, is the foundation of American AI leadership.
As of the end of 2025, just five American companies held over 70% of global AI compute.
4Luke Emberson, Josh You, and Venkat Somala, “Five Hyperscalers Now Own Over Two-Thirds of Global AI Compute,” Epoch AI, April 14, 2026.

This dominance is a major frustration for America’s adversaries, who are highly dependent on this supply chain. This is especially true of the CCP, which openly aspires to acquire equivalent or superior capabilities across the complex chip manufacturing process. The U.S. Intelligence Community’s 2025 Annual Threat Assessment report expresses high confidence that China “has a multifaceted, national-level strategy designed to displace the United States as the world’s most influential AI power by 2030.”5Office of the Director of National Intelligence, 2025 Annual Threat Assessment of the U.S. Intelligence Community, March 18, 2025.
The CCP explicitly makes AI capability the centerpiece of its military strategy, identifying AI progress as its best chance to mitigate and perhaps exceed American military superiority.6Sam Bresnick, China’s Military AI Roadblocks: PRC Perspectives on Technological Challenges to Intelligentized Warfare, Center for Security and Emerging Technologies, June 2024. AI’s potential to become a new general-purpose technology also represents an opportunity for compounding economic benefit. The State Council of China’s stated goal is to “promote the broad and deep integration of artificial intelligence with all sectors and domains of the economy and society” for this reason.7State Council of the People’s Republic of China, “Opinions of the State Council on Deepening the Implementation of the ‘Artificial Intelligence Plus’ Initiative,” August 26, 2025. The CCP is particularly focused on using AI to supercharge its advanced manufacturing capabilities.
Despite its military and economic ambitions, China currently lags meaningfully on chip design and production. Export controls on chips and SME have helped constrain China’s ability to close this gap.8Export controls have contributed to a fivefold advantage over China in total AI computational capacity; see Oren Cass, “Winning the AI Arms Race against the Chinese Communist Party,” testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, January 14, 2026. The Trump administration’s 2025 AI Action Plan endorses this approach: “Advanced AI compute is essential to the AI era, enabling both economic dynamism and novel military capabilities. Denying our foreign adversaries access to this resource, then, is a matter of both geostrategic competition and national security.”9The White House, America’s AI Action Plan, July 2025.
Yet in practice, American controls are limited. A House Select Committee on China report highlights the problem:

articles.summary: Applied Materials opens $5B semiconductor innovation center  Manufacturing Dive
articles.full_text:
Dive Brief:
- Applied Materials, an equipment, services and software supplier for chipmakers, has opened its multibillion-dollar Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization Center to collaborate with industry on next-generation technologies.
- Leading chipmakers, systems companies, equipment partners and research universities will work at the center to develop advanced chipmaking processes, as well as to move technologies from early-stage research to high-volume manufacturing faster, Applied Materials said.
- The 600,000-square-foot facility is located at the company’s campus in Sunnyvale, California, and has near four acres of advanced cleanroom space. Applied Materials said it expects capital spending to reach $5 billion as new customer projects begin.
Dive Insight:
The news comes several months after Applied Materials announced it had partnered with South Korea-based SK Hynix to accelerate memory innovation and address semiconductor-related challenges at the EPIC Center. The agreement was reached as technology firms navigate a global shortage of memory chips driven by surging artificial intelligence demand.
According to Applied Materials, the EPIC Center will “reinvent” the standard research and development model in the semiconductor industry. The standard model typically involves handing off foundational materials research, equipment and process development, and process integration and pilot produciton from one siloed environment to the next.
“The EPIC Center is designed to remove these handoffs, putting the people who invent the materials, build the equipment, and make the chips together in a state-of-the-art facility purpose-built for commercialization,” the company said. “The technologies the AI era demands are too complex and too consequential for any one company to invent alone.”
Applied Materials said it expects the center’s operating model to provide chipmakers early access to advanced materials and equipment, shorter learning cycles and a faster path to volume production.
Materials innovation has “outgrown serial development” and “demands coordinated development and integrated solutions,” Prabu Raja, president of Applied Materials’ semiconductor products group, said in a statement. “EPIC is the only place where materials, process technology and equipment will be innovated in parallel, which increases the success rate of new materials and technologies.”
Partners in the EPIC Center “span the AI technology stack” and include TSMC, Intel, SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung Electronics, Broadcom and Advantest, along with Arizona State University, Stanford University, University of California, Berkeley and other institutions. More companies and organizations are expected to join the center over time.
Applied Materials reported $7.01 billion in Q1 revenue, above the midpoint of its guided range, citing increased demand for leading-edge logic, high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging.

South Korea's KOSDAQ-listed Nexadynamics has secured a 31.1084 billion won (approximately $23.1 million) contract to supply high-performance AI servers to a South Korean artificial intelligence (AI) specialist firm. The amount represents 239.06% of the company's consolidated revenue last year (13.01287 billion won, or approximately $9.7 million), and following last month's order from a Japanese company, the addition of domestic volume is accelerating the company's pivot toward the AI infrastructure business.
According to the Financial Supervisory Service's electronic disclosure system on the 15th, the contract period runs six months through April 14 next year, with products supplied on a merchandise sales basis. The counterparty was not disclosed at the request of trade secret protection.
The payment structure is designed with a 30% down payment and 70% balance. The company will receive approximately 9.33 billion won (approximately $6.9 million) as a down payment upon signing, which it will use as working capital for procuring high-cost components. The remaining balance will be collected in stages aligned with product shipment and delivery schedules, reducing the likelihood of uncollected receivables.
This order marks the first major achievement since the management reshuffle completed at an extraordinary shareholders' meeting in September. Nexadynamics reorganized its board with semiconductor, telecommunications, and data center experts, led by CEO Lee Kang-chil, a former SK Hynix vice president, alongside inside director Lee Dong-han from Intel Korea, outside director Kim Hu-jong, former head of SK Telecom's Service Technology Center and executive director at Huawei, inside director Lee Sang-min, former LG Uplus technology division head and AI professor at Gachon University, and director Hwang Dong-woo from data center specialist DC Korea.
Since the new management took office, order momentum has continued across both domestic and international markets. Last month, the company signed a $1.15 million (approximately 1.6 billion won) contract with a Japanese IT firm to supply AI servers and accessories. Including this latest South Korean contract, the two recent orders total approximately 32.7 billion won (approximately $24.3 million).
The company is also accelerating the build-out of its own production base alongside product supply. Using proceeds from a 13 billion won (approximately $9.6 million) rights offering completed last month, Nexadynamics is constructing a dedicated AI GPU server assembly line spanning approximately 2,000 pyeong (about 71,000 square feet) at the Sihwa National Industrial Complex. Trial production is planned for the fourth quarter of this year, with full-scale mass production beginning next year.
Through this, the company aims to expand into the enterprise AI data center and high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure markets, with a goal of transforming into a comprehensive AI infrastructure solutions provider by 2027. In particular, it is cultivating finished GPU server products for AI data centers as its next growth engine.
A Nexadynamics representative said, "This supply contract is evidence that the market has confidence in our technology sourcing capabilities and financial stability, and a symbolic milestone signaling a full-scale turnaround. We will strive to enhance shareholder value through stable product delivery and further expansion of domestic and international AI infrastructure orders."

articles.title: South Korea's Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix Enter Value-Buying Zone as PBR Falls to Around 1.5x - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: South Korea's Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix Enter Value-Buying Zone as PBR Falls to Around 1.5x  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix shares continue to languish despite record earnings, and an analysis suggests both companies' price-to-book ratios (PBR) have fallen to around 1.5x, entering a value-buying zone. Song Jong-ho, CEO of TechInsight Investment and a former head of SK Hynix's Future Strategy Division, said in an interview on the 13th, "Semiconductor stocks are completely undervalued right now," emphasizing that "this is a zone where you need to catch the bottom."
He pointed out that during the July stock decline, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both rebounded at 1.5x their projected 2027 book value per share (BPS). He believes current prices are approaching similar levels based on next year's projected BPS. He estimated Samsung Electronics' projected BPS for next year at approximately 170,000 won (approximately $130) and SK Hynix's at approximately 1 million won (approximately $750). Given that SK Hynix's stock is trading in the 1.4 million to 1.5 million won range (approximately $1,000 to $1,100), the PBR has come down to around 1.5x.
The valuation framework he presented is as follows:
| Company | Projected 2027 BPS | Stock Price | PBR | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung Electronics | ~170,000 won | 262,000 won | ~1.5x | 
| SK Hynix | ~1 million won | 1.4M–1.5M won range | ~1.4–1.5x | 
Samsung Electronics' stock price is based on the October 8 closing price, when preliminary earnings were released.
Foreign investor capital flight was cited as the key reason why South Korean semiconductor stocks have failed to gain traction despite strong earnings. With interest rates above 5%, foreign investors are reducing their exposure to emerging markets including South Korea. Samsung Electronics' foreign ownership has fallen to the 46% range, the lowest level in about 18 years since the global financial crisis.
The foreign exodus is not limited to Samsung Electronics. According to Korea Exchange data, SK Hynix's foreign ownership has also fallen to 49.59%, dipping below 50% for the first time since 2023. Foreign investors have net sold more than 197 trillion won (approximately $147.0 billion) worth of KOSPI stocks this year. That compares with net buying of 11 trillion won (approximately $8.2 billion) in 2023, a flat position in 2024, and 4 trillion won (approximately $3.0 billion) in 2025—a completely different order of magnitude.
Song nevertheless stressed that the AI industry is still in the middle stages of growth, and investors should not dismiss the potential for future upside based solely on short-term price declines. He shared that during the COVID-19 crash, he bought Tesla shares and saw the price double within three months.
Semiconductor industry: innings 5–6 of a 9-inning game
He used a baseball analogy to explain why semiconductor earnings are improving but stock prices are not rising. The AI industry is roughly in the 4th inning of a 9-inning game, while the semiconductor industry is in the 5th or 6th inning. Since semiconductors are a cyclical industry, concerns that the upcycle may soon turn or that investment may slow are weighing on stock prices. He also cited improving earnings and expanding market share among Chinese competitors as a burden.
To alleviate these concerns, strong shareholder return policies are needed, and he noted that stock prices appear to have turned weak recently as share buyback programs concluded.
On the possibility of further improvement in semiconductor conditions, he drew a line, saying, "With revenue and operating profit already rising steeply, it's difficult to maintain the same growth pace." However, he noted that TSMC has built consensus through consistent earnings surprises that foundry is not simply a cyclical industry but a sustainably growing one. Memory semiconductors now stand at a similar crossroads, he said. If Samsung Electronics surpasses 150 trillion won (approximately $111.9 billion) in quarterly operating profit next year, the stock is unlikely to stay at current levels, and foreign capital could flow back in large volumes, he predicted.
Samsung Electronics relatively better positioned in HBM4 competition
On the Chinese semiconductor catch-up, he acknowledged that "for noise, it seems to be dealing a fairly significant blow," but assessed that Chinese memory companies still need more time to catch up with South Korea. CXMT has yet to enter the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) market, and its aggressive capacity expansion is concentrated in commodity memory rather than high-value-added products, meaning a technology gap still exists.
However, he added that given precedents in secondary batteries and shipbuilding where Chinese companies rapidly caught up with South Korea, there is considerable wariness in the semiconductor industry as well. He questioned whether Chinese companies could enter next-generation high-value markets such as high-bandwidth flash (HBF) beyond HBM in the short term.
HBF standardization is being led by SK Hynix together with SanDisk through the Open Compute Project (OCP). The two companies released their first technical specifications in August 2026. Japan's Kioxia, on the NAND side, also unveiled a high-bandwidth flash module prototype with 5TB capacity and 64GB per second bandwidth in August 2025, targeting the same market.
When asked to compare the investment appeal of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, he said the key is which company secures leadership in the HBM4 market. He assessed that Samsung Electronics has recently been closing the gap with SK Hynix in both technology and earnings, increasing its competitiveness. HBM market share last year was SK Hynix 60%, Samsung Electronics and Micron 20% each, but this year it has shifted to 50%, 30%, and 20%, and next year he expects SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics to each hold 40%, with Micron at 20%.
His HBM market share forecast is as follows:
| Period | SK Hynix | Samsung Electronics | Micron | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 2025 | 60% | 20% | 20% | 
| 2026 | 50% | 30% | 20% | 
| 2027 (forecast) | 40% | 40% | 20% | 
Actual revenue-based market share data compiled by market research firm Counterpoint Research shows a similar trend. In Q2 2026, the HBM market was SK Hynix 50%, Samsung Electronics 33%, and Micron 18%, not far off from this year's forecast. In the same tally, overall DRAM share was Samsung Electronics 38%, SK Hynix 25%, and Micron 24%, with China's CXMT at 10%, more than doubling from 4% a year earlier.
Since the market assigns higher value to companies expanding market share, Samsung Electronics is relatively better positioned, he said. He also cited the foundry business as a variable. Samsung Electronics' foundry division is expected to post a loss of about 1 trillion won (approximately $746.1 million) this year, but if it turns profitable next year, the company's valuation could be reassessed higher.
This is also where memory competition intersects with foundry competition. HBM places a base die (logic die) that serves as a controller beneath the DRAM die. Starting with HBM4, SK Hynix outsources this logic die to TSMC, while Samsung Electronics produces it in-house at its 4nm foundry. In fact, HBM4 base die production recently surpassed 50% of Samsung Electronics' 4nm foundry capacity, which is cited as a factor reducing foundry losses.
When asked whether it's reasonable to start dollar-cost averaging at current prices, he answered "yes." Both companies have entered a zone of lower PBRs, and based on projected BPS for next year and the year after, there are even periods where valuations fall to around 1.1x.
South Korean materials, components, and equipment: need to separate winners from losers
On South Korean materials, components, and equipment companies, he assessed that new entry is somewhat burdensome at current levels. Since U.S. materials, components, and equipment companies are far larger than their South Korean counterparts, he stressed that separating winners from losers is critical in the domestic market. He particularly advised watching companies that have succeeded in localizing equipment previously dependent on overseas suppliers.
As a representative example, he cited KOSDAQ-listed VM. The company localized etching equipment used to remove unnecessary material in semiconductor circuit fabrication—a field previously monopolized by U.S.-based Lam Research and Japan's Tokyo Electron. VM has succeeded in localization and is now supplying equipment to SK Hynix and others.
Cerebras as the next-generation AI semiconductor leader
On the assessment that Nvidia's monopoly in the AI semiconductor market is weakening, he diagnosed that the monopoly began to crack starting in 2024. However, he drew a line, saying Nvidia remains the dominant player leading AI infrastructure innovation and investment. He believes the "next Nvidia" is most likely to emerge from Big Tech, with Google currently the most likely candidate.
He also forecast that AI will evolve beyond agents to artificial general intelligence (AGI) and physical AI. Google is vertically integrating not only software but also AI infrastructure, and is developing vision-language-action (VLA) models needed for robots to understand visual information and translate it into action, he explained. He predicted that after generative AI, dependence on Google and Nvidia technology will remain high in the robotics and humanoid robot markets.
Among other AI semiconductor companies to watch, he highlighted Cerebras Systems. As the center of gravity in the AI industry shifts from training to inference, computing architecture is changing, and the role of neural processing units (NPUs) specialized for inference is growing alongside GPUs.
Globally, there are about 9 to 10 companies developing NPUs, but he assessed that only a handful have actually mass-produced chips, have experience using TSMC's foundry, and have the potential to supply data centers. BOK's Shin highlights need to curb inflation amid chip boom, Middle East conflict
Bank of Korea Gov. Shin Hyun-song cited the need to “get inflation down,” and added that getting monetary policy right was “absolutely key” ahead of next week’s rate meeting.
Bank of Korea Gov. Shin Hyun-song discusses inflation and economic pressures during a CNN Global Perspectives session in Bangkok on Oct. 14.SCREEN CAPTURE
The chief of the Bank of Korea (BOK) on Wednesday stressed the importance of keeping inflation under control, saying the global AI investment boom and the prolonged Middle East conflict are combining to push up consumer prices.
“Korea sits at the intersection of two of the most important trends right now. One is AI and the big investment boom, and the other one is the war in the Middle East,” BOK Gov. Shin Hyun-song said during a CNN Global Perspectives session livestreamed online on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Group (IMF-WBG) annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
“In terms of activity, they pull in opposite directions. But the AI economy is swamping the negative effect of the war in the Middle East. But in terms of inflation, and this is relevant for the central bank, they are actually combining to raise inflation,” he said.
Korea is at the forefront of the global AI boom, as demand for AI computing infrastructure has fueled demand for memory chips, driving exports and profits at the country's two major chipmakers, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, to record highs.
However, export-driven growth has raised concerns that the benefits of the semiconductor boom have not fully spilled over into the broader economy, deepening economic polarization and contributing to what is known as a K-shaped economy.
“We do, in fact, have a pretty sharp case of a K-shaped economy,” Shin said, adding that people in the lowest income group are hit hardest by inflation.
“I think the best thing from a central bank perspective is to just keep in mind that inflation hurts the lowest-income members of the population most,” he said. “So this is why we need to get inflation down, and getting monetary policy right is absolutely key.”
His remarks come as the BOK has tightened monetary policy to address inflationary pressures, with inflation remaining above its 2 percent target.
The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate to 3 percent through consecutive hikes at its July and August meetings, describing the moves as “pre-emptive” measures to prevent inflationary pressures from accelerating further.
The BOK will hold its next rate-setting meeting next week.

articles.title: CXMT’s 4F² DRAM Plan Jolts Korean Chipmakers - Businesskorea
articles.summary: CXMT’s 4F² DRAM Plan Jolts Korean Chipmakers  Businesskorea
articles.full_text:
Experts say CXMT's mass production of 4F² DRAM is still years away, while Samsung and SK hynix have also been developing the technology on their own
As China’s largest memory semiconductor company, ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), announced the release of server DRAM applied with the next-generation DRAM cell structure ‘4F² (Four F Square)’ new technology within this year, the global semiconductor market has plunged into a fierce storm.
The high-performance memory market for servers is a core territory that has been led by a few semiconductor giants in South Korea and the United States, such as Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron. As China’s CXMT, which has mainly focused on producing general-purpose products, threw down the gauntlet in this area, fears spread that the memory technology gap is narrowing much faster than expected. In the aftermath, a massive shockwave was created in the domestic stock market, freezing investor sentiment as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix faced record plunges reaching the 7% range and the 10% range, respectively.
Amidst this escalating sense of crisis in the market, Song Jae-hyuk, President and Chief Technology Officer (CTO) of the Device Solutions (DS) Unit at Samsung Electronics, stepped in to extinguish the fire at the 28th Semiconductor Exhibition (SEDEX) held at COEX in Seoul on Oct. 14. When asked by reporters whether Samsung Electronics is also developing 4F², President Song clearly answered, “Yes.” Regarding the progress of the development, he spared his words, stating, “We are working hard,” but implied that the domestic industry has also already been preparing the corresponding technology from multiple angles.
In fact, 4F² is a technology that the domestic semiconductor dual carriage, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, have early on researched as a core pillar of future processes. SK hynix previously revealed its plan to introduce the 4F² VG (Vertical Gate) platform in the sub-10-nanometer segment at a symposium, and Samsung Electronics also successfully manufactured a 16Gb DRAM test chip with a 4F² structure and achieved actual operation at the International Solid-State Circuits Conference.
Does CXMT’s forecasted release within this year immediately mean the overtaking of South Korea’s technology? Experts point out the need to coldly examine the truth and falsehood of the announcement’s contents.
According to academic experts, the plan announced by CXMT entirely omits expressions such as full-scale mass production or sample supply. Even the specific product specifications or release schedules containing the reality of commercialization have not been disclosed. Therefore, analysis suggests it is reasonable to interpret this not as a signal flare for full-scale mass production, but as a release preview tinged with political and marketing purposes. Since server DRAM must go through difficult yield securing and strict quality certification processes by major client companies apart from prototype production, the timing for large-scale mass production in a practical sense is predicted to be possible at the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028 at the earliest.
4F² is a technology that drastically reduces the area occupied by a single memory cell. F is the minimum line width that serves as the standard for circuit processing, and compared to the current mainstream 6F² (width 3F and length 2F), 4F² (width and length 2F each) reduces the area by about 30% and improves the theoretical integration density by 50%. However, changing the structure does not immediately mean the realization of ultra-high integration.
While the line width of the 4F² cell that China’s CXMT intends to apply is currently at the 15-nanometer (nm) level, the current 6F² cell focused on by the domestic memory industry is at the 12.2-nanometer level, keeping the actual integration density realized by the two technologies at a similar level. Although China is breathlessly chasing through structural reorganization, the prevailing diagnosis is that it is unreasonable to conclude that they have surpassed South Korea by more than two years in terms of technical completeness.
Behind CXMT throwing the 4F² winning move lies the United States’ high-intensity export controls on extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment. While Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix draw fine circuits through advanced EUV equipment, China is blocked from securing EUV and must rely on multi-patterning, which repeatedly overlaps and engraves circuits using deep ultraviolet (DUV) equipment. Choosing the smaller-area 4F² structure becomes a realistic escape route for China because it allows them to bypass and achieve a certain level of integration density even with a relatively large line width. However, as the price for not being able to use EUV, it is difficult to make vertical channel transistors uniform, and numerous difficult challenges are blocking the way, such as current leakage, the floating body effect, and wafer bonding. For this reason, technological pessimism coexists, suggesting that the initial yield could fall below 10%.
However, leading semiconductor scholars warn that as China experiences these difficult challenges as if banging their heads against a brick wall, they could gain unexpected nourishment in the future next-generation three-dimensional (3D) DRAM competition. It is a stark reality that the time gap South Korea has earned due to US sanctions is gradually narrowing. The fact that domestic semiconductor leaders, including the Samsung Electronics CTO and the SK hynix President of Development, toured partner booths together and strengthened their solidarity at the event venue also reflects this sense of crisis.
Currently, to counter China’s pursuit, the South Korean semiconductor camp is staking its life on ultra-gap technologies for high value-added AI memory, such as the HBM5 conceptual model beyond the 7th generation High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) HBM4E, and technology that combines AI computation functions into memory. As China has chased right up to the chin with a structural transformation that bypasses EUV sanctions, it is time for the government and the industry to move beyond simple fear and further accelerate overwhelming yield competitiveness and the speed of developing next-generation source technologies.

articles.title: Dan Ives’ AI Bull Case Extends To South Korea – With A 9,000 KOSPI Target And 2027 Stock Picks - TradingView
articles.summary: Dan Ives’ AI Bull Case Extends To South Korea – With A 9,000 KOSPI Target And 2027 Stock Picks  TradingView

The South Korean stock market could hit fresh all-time highs over the next six to 12 months as concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) have triggered an excessive selloff, according to analyst Dan Ives. The Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director sees further upside in Korean semiconductor companies, expects U.S. technology stocks to rise through 2029 and has named five stocks he favors for 2027.
KOSPI Selloff Creates Buying Opportunity
“South Korea reminds me of Silicon Valley in the mid-1990s,” Ives said during a press conference in Seoul on Wednesday. He added that global AI investment remains in its early stages and that investors are underestimating the role of South Korean companies in the AI ecosystem.
Ives expects the KOSPI to recover to around 9,000 within the next six to 12 months. “Four years ago, small Wall Street financial firms didn’t even know what the KOSPI was, but now even New York taxi drivers do,” Ives said.
However, the index turned negative on Wednesday after rising as much as 2.6% earlier in the session. South Korea-focused exchange-traded funds also came under pressure. The Direxion Daily South Korea Bull 3X Shares (KORU) fell more than 4% in the premarket session, while the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY), which tracks large- and mid-cap South Korean equities, declined 1.3%.
Samsung, SK Hynix Undervalued
Ives believes South Korean semiconductor giants SK Hynix Inc. (SKHY) and Samsung Electronics (SSNLF) are undervalued relative to their fundamentals.
Ives also pushed back against concerns about capacity expansion and technological advances by Chinese memory-chip makers, including ChangXin Memory Technologies. He said South Korean companies remain at least three years ahead of their Chinese competitors.
He acknowledged that China could narrow the gap and eventually develop competitive solutions, but said concerns about Chinese competition hurting South Korean memory-chip companies were overblown.
Nasdaq Could Reach 35,000 By 2029
Ives also predicted that U.S. large-cap tech stocks could see their valuations rise by an average of 30% by 2029 as AI investment expands.
“The fourth industrial revolution led by AI is only about 15% complete,” he said, adding that the Nasdaq could reach 35,000 by 2029. The tech-heavy index closed at 27,204.38 on Oct. 13, implying a potential gain of about 29.6% over the next three years if it reaches that level.
Ives Names Five Tech Stocks For 2027
Looking ahead to 2027, Ives identified Nvidia (NVDA), Microsoft (MSFT), Palantir (PLTR), Apple (AAPL) and CrowdStrike (CRWD) as his top five technology stock picks. He also expressed optimism about Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX), predicting an 80% probability that the two companies will merge within the next 12 months.
“Musk’s plan is to bring all AI companies under one roof, and this entity will become the world’s largest hyperscaler,” Ives said.
How Korean Markets Have Fared In 2026
South Korean stocks have rallied sharply this year, with the KOSPI up more than 42% year-to-date. Similarly, EWY has climbed around 70%, while KORU has gained over 59%.

Applied Materials Launches $5 Billion EPIC Center With Samsung, SK hynix, TSMC and Intel As CXMT Mass Production Claim Shakes Markets and Gains Ground
While global stock markets fluctuated over the news of China’s world-first mass production of DRAM within the year, global semiconductor companies including Samsung Electronics have formed a research and development (R&D) alliance to launch a counterattack. In particular, Samsung Electronics showcased its status and strength as the top memory semiconductor company by unveiling advanced semiconductors in collaboration with Nvidia and AMD.

articles.summary: Jeonbuk Bank Launches South Korea’s First Bitcoin-Backed Corporate Loans  Serrari Group
articles.full_text:
Share
Jeonbuk Bank, a subsidiary of JB Financial Group, has introduced Bitcoin-backed loans for corporate customers in South Korea. Businesses can borrow Korean won for operating expenses using Bitcoin as collateral, while registered third-party custodians hold the cryptocurrency. The launch follows changes to civil enforcement rules that provide a court-supervised route for selling digital assets when borrowers default.
Key Overview
- Lender: Jeonbuk Bank, part of JB Financial Group.
- Eligible borrowers: Corporate customers.
- Accepted collateral: Bitcoin only at launch.
- Loan currency: South Korean won.
- Permitted use: Business operating expenses.
- Custody arrangement: Registered third-party digital asset custodians.
- Default recovery: Court-supervised sale of pledged Bitcoin.
Jeonbuk Bank Introduces Bitcoin-Backed Business Loans
Jeonbuk Bank has launched a lending service that allows corporate customers to borrow Korean won using Bitcoin as collateral, marking a first for South Korea’s traditional banking sector. The regional lender is initially restricting the product to businesses seeking working capital, rather than offering cryptocurrency-backed loans to individual consumers.
The initiative introduces a new way for companies holding Bitcoin to access financing without immediately selling their digital assets. Under the arrangement, borrowers pledge Bitcoin to secure a loan, while the bank provides funding in Korean won.
The service is part of Jeonbuk Bank’s wider effort to develop digital asset financial services. The bank’s first bank-issued won loans backed by Bitcoin also establish a framework for handling cryptocurrency collateral within conventional banking procedures.
The initial rollout is deliberately narrow: Bitcoin is the only accepted digital asset, and loan proceeds must be used for business operations. The bank may consider expanding the service as it gains experience and as regulations and customer demand evolve.
How the Bitcoin-Backed Loans Work
The arrangement separates lending from cryptocurrency custody. Businesses pledge Bitcoin as collateral, but Jeonbuk Bank does not directly own or manage the pledged coins. Instead, a registered custodian holds the assets while the bank manages the lending relationship and assesses the collateral.
This structure allows the lender to provide financing without operating its own Bitcoin custody system. The registered crypto custody provider holds the collateral, while the bank retains a claim secured by the pledged assets.
Bitcoin was selected because of its market size, trading activity and liquidity, which provide a broader basis for valuing the collateral and assessing whether it can be sold if a borrower fails to repay.
The bank has developed its own valuation system using prices from multiple cryptocurrency exchanges alongside market volatility indicators. This approach is designed to reduce dependence on a single exchange’s price and help the lender assess collateral during volatile market conditions.
However, the bank has not publicly disclosed key commercial terms, including interest rates, borrowing limits, loan-to-value ratios or the identity of the custodian.
Court Procedures Provide a Route to Recover Unpaid Loans
A central feature of the service is how the bank can recover its money if a borrower defaults. South Korea’s revised Civil Execution Rules, which took effect on 1 October 2026, provide procedures for enforcing claims involving virtual assets.
If a company fails to repay its loan, Jeonbuk Bank can pursue a court-ordered sale of the bitcoin pledged as collateral. The proceeds can then be used to settle the outstanding debt without the bank needing to take direct possession of the cryptocurrency.
This legal process distinguishes the service from some cryptocurrency lending arrangements that automatically liquidate collateral when preset price thresholds are reached. Jeonbuk Bank’s model instead relies on custody arrangements, loan agreements and court-supervised enforcement.
The framework provides a route for recovering funds, but it does not eliminate lending risks. Bitcoin prices can fall sharply, and the amount recovered from a forced sale may be insufficient to cover the outstanding loan. The timing and outcome of enforcement also matter.

Risk Management and Collateral Valuation
Bitcoin’s volatility presents a central challenge for any lender accepting it as security. If the asset’s market value declines substantially, the collateral may no longer adequately cover the borrower’s obligations.
Jeonbuk Bank has conducted stress tests to examine how Bitcoin collateral could perform during sharp price declines. It also reviewed loan-to-value ratios and margin-call thresholds while designing the product.
These measures are intended to help the bank assess potential losses and determine how collateral should be valued. The use of prices from multiple exchanges can also help reduce the influence of unusual price movements on any one trading platform.
Custody is another important part of the risk framework. The bank’s arrangements rely on eligible providers that must meet South Korea’s relevant security and regulatory requirements, including applicable safeguards for customer assets.
Still, important details remain undisclosed. Without public information on collateral requirements, interest rates, margin procedures and borrowing limits, businesses cannot fully assess the financing costs and risks associated with the product.
A Potential Expansion of Digital Asset Banking
Jeonbuk Bank’s launch could provide a model for other financial institutions exploring ways to incorporate digital assets into conventional lending. The bank is beginning with corporate borrowers and a single cryptocurrency, giving it an opportunity to assess how collateral valuation, custody and enforcement work in practice.
The lender has indicated that it will review whether to broaden eligible borrowers, accepted assets and services based on market demand and regulatory developments. For now, individual customers cannot access the loans.
The development also reflects wider interest in using digital assets as collateral for institutional financing. However, Jeonbuk Bank’s initial offering remains distinct from consumer crypto lending and does not establish that other South Korean banks will immediately introduce similar products.
Outlook
Jeonbuk Bank’s Bitcoin-backed corporate loans introduce a new financing option for South Korean businesses that hold digital assets. By allowing companies to borrow Korean won against Bitcoin, the lender provides a way to access working capital without requiring an immediate sale of the cryptocurrency.
The model’s success will depend on the effectiveness of its collateral valuation, custody arrangements and recovery procedures. Bitcoin’s price volatility remains a significant risk, while the undisclosed loan terms make it difficult to assess the product’s full cost and suitability for businesses.
The court-supervised recovery framework provides a legal route for handling defaults, but it does not guarantee that collateral sales will cover every outstanding loan. The bank will also need to demonstrate that its risk controls remain effective during periods of market stress.
For now, the launch represents an initial step in bringing digital assets into conventional corporate lending. Any broader adoption will depend on operational results, regulatory developments and whether the bank can manage cryptocurrency-related risks within its existing lending framework.

2. Can individuals apply for these loans?
No. The initial service is limited to corporate customers seeking funding for business operations.
3. Does Jeonbuk Bank hold the Bitcoin directly?
No. Registered third-party digital asset custodians hold the pledged Bitcoin while the bank provides the loan.
4. What happens if a borrower defaults?
The bank can pursue a court-supervised sale of the pledged Bitcoin and use the proceeds to recover the outstanding debt.

articles.title: IMF World Economic Outlook sharply upgrades South Korea to 3.3%, downgrades Latin America - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: IMF World Economic Outlook sharply upgrades South Korea to 3.3%, downgrades Latin America  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
IMF Raises Global Growth Forecast to 3.1%... South Korea 3.3%, Taiwan 10.7% on 'AI Boom'
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised its global economic growth forecast for this year by 0.1 percentage point, from 3.0% to 3.1%. The revision reflects the fund's assessment that the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) investment is offsetting downward pressure from the prolonged Middle East war and trade conflicts, keeping the global economy on a better-than-expected trajectory.
In its October World Economic Outlook released on the 13th, the IMF sharply upgraded growth forecasts for South Korea and Taiwan, which sit at the heart of the AI hardware and semiconductor supply chain. South Korea's real GDP growth forecast for this year was raised by 0.7 percentage point, from 2.6% in July to 3.3%. Given that the April forecast stood at just 1.9%, the projection has climbed a full 1.4 percentage points in only six months.
Taiwan's upward revision is even steeper. The IMF now projects Taiwan's growth this year at 10.7%, a jump of 5.5 percentage points from the April forecast of 5.2%. Next year's growth forecast was also raised by 1.3 percentage points to 4.3%.
In its report, the IMF identified South Korea and Taiwan as key trading economies for AI-related computer hardware, noting that the two economies account for 62% of net trade in that sector. On South Korea, the fund said "strong external demand for semiconductors will support growth momentum, offsetting the negative impact of the war."
South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance attributed the upgrade to "the impact of robust AI hardware and semiconductor-related export performance." If this forecast materializes, South Korea's growth rate would surpass that of the United States for the first time in four years, since 2022.
AI Value Chain Participation Divides Growth Paths
The IMF assessed that country-level growth trajectories will diverge depending on exposure to the Middle East war and the degree of participation in the AI technology value chain. This bifurcation is clearly visible in the growth gap between advanced economies and emerging and developing economies.
The growth forecast for the advanced economy group (41 countries) was revised up by 0.4 percentage point from July to 2.1%, while the emerging and developing economy group—comprising 155 countries including China, India, Russia, and Brazil—saw its growth forecast lowered by 0.1 percentage point to 3.7%.
The U.S. growth forecast for this year was held at 2.3%. The fund judged that big tech-led technology investment and productivity strength are underpinning growth, limiting the war's impact. The Eurozone was upgraded from 0.9% to 1.1%, and Japan from 0.6% to 0.7%, but both are still expected to fall short of last year's growth rates (1.2% each) due to weakened consumer sentiment from energy burdens.
China's growth forecast for this year was revised down from 4.6% to 4.5%, with the 5% threshold—long viewed as a psychological line in the sand—now expected to be breached.
Latin America Downgraded... Energy Shock Takes Direct Hit
Latin America and the Caribbean, largely left out of the AI boom, saw growth forecasts lowered across the board. The IMF projects the region's growth this year at 2.3%, down from last year's 2.5% and the July forecast of 2.4%. Next year's forecast was also cut from 2.7% to 2.5%.
The IMF noted that "most countries in the region have little offsetting benefit from the technology upcycle." With Brent crude prices holding roughly 45% above pre-war levels due to the Middle East conflict, energy-importing countries face mounting burdens on households and businesses.
Among major economies, Argentina saw the steepest downgrade. This year's growth forecast was cut by 1.4 percentage points, from 3.5% in July to 2.1%, and next year's was adjusted from 4.0% to 3.5%. Inflation, however, is expected to moderate from 41.9% last year to 32.5% this year.
Brazil's growth forecast for this year was lowered from 2.4% to 2.2%, and next year's from 2.2% to 1.9%. The IMF cited tight monetary policy aimed at returning inflation to target, reduced government fiscal support, and global uncertainty as factors weighing on growth.
Mexico was an exception, with this year's forecast raised from 1.2% to 1.5%. The fund attributed this to export and investment stabilization through the AI supply chain. Next year's forecast, however, was trimmed slightly from 1.9% to 1.8%.
The following table summarizes the IMF's October forecast revisions for major economies.
| Country/Region | October Forecast | July Forecast | Revision | 
|---|---|---|---|
| South Korea | 3.3% | 2.6% | +0.7%p | 
| Taiwan | 10.7% | 5.2%* | +5.5%p* | 
| United States | 2.3% | 2.3% | 0.0%p | 
| Eurozone | 1.1% | 0.9% | +0.2%p | 
| Japan | 0.7% | 0.6% | +0.1%p | 
| China | 4.5% | 4.6% | -0.1%p | 
| Argentina | 2.1% | 3.5% | -1.4%p | 
| Brazil | 2.2% | 2.4% | -0.2%p | 
| Mexico | 1.5% | 1.2% | +0.3%p | 
Note: Taiwan's July figure is based on the April forecast (5.2%), as the IMF publishes revised forecasts for only 30 major economies in July.
Downside Risks Remain... IMF Urges Vigilance on Inflation and Fiscal Discipline
The IMF assessed that risks to the global economy remain tilted to the downside. It identified commodity price volatility, inflationary pressure, the possibility of a reassessment of AI productivity expectations, and a resurgence of trade frictions as key risk factors. The fund warned in particular that prolonged conflicts in the Middle East and elsewhere could reignite inflationary pressure, and that any adjustment in expectations for AI-driven productivity gains could lead to reduced investment.
The global inflation forecast for this year was held at 4.7%. This outlook is premised on the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz in November and the normalization of energy supply and logistics by February next year.
The IMF recommended that countries build fiscal buffers, pursue medium-term fiscal consolidation, and focus fiscal policy on temporary and targeted support for vulnerable populations. It also urged monetary policy that prioritizes price stability above all else.
South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance stated: "Alongside the prolonged Middle East war, rising prices and interest rates continue to burden livelihoods, while structural issues such as polarization and slowing potential growth persist." The ministry added that it "plans to devote full efforts to easing polarization, stabilizing livelihoods, and rebounding potential growth, including through the promotion of three core social policies: housing, jobs, and grassroots finance."
