Summary:
- Japan’s corporate goods price index rose 6.8% year on year in September, below the 7.6% forecast and August’s 7.6% gain, but still at an elevated level
- On the month, prices fell 0.3%, against expectations for a 0.5% rise, following a 0.2% decline in August
- Companies continued to pass on higher fuel and chemical costs to each other
- The yen-based import price index jumped 24.5% year on year, showing the weak currency is still pushing up the cost of raw material imports
- The data keep alive market expectations of a near-term Bank of Japan rate hike, with the board due to publish new growth and inflation forecasts at this month’s meeting
Japan’s wholesale prices rose 6.8% in the year to September as companies passed on higher fuel and chemical costs, data released by the Bank of Japan showed on Tuesday, keeping inflationary pressure elevated and market expectations of a near-term interest rate hike alive.
The annual increase in the corporate goods price index, which tracks the prices companies charge each other for goods and services, fell short of the median market forecast of 7.6% and was below August’s 7.6% rise. On a monthly basis, prices fell 0.3%, against expectations for a 0.5% increase, after a 0.2% drop in August.
The headline miss offers the central bank only limited comfort. An annual pace near 7% remains well above levels consistent with the BOJ’s price goals, and the details point to continued cost pressure feeding through supply chains.
The clearest sign of that pressure came from import costs. The yen-based import price index surged 24.5% from a year earlier, showing that the currency’s weakness continues to inflate the cost of raw materials Japan brings in from abroad. With energy prices high, a soft yen magnifies the impact, raising the domestic cost of fuel and other inputs that companies then pass on to customers.
The data will be among the factors the BOJ board weighs when it produces fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts at its policy meeting later this month. Wholesale prices tend to lead consumer inflation, as firms gradually pass higher input costs on to households, which makes the pipeline readings an important guide for policymakers assessing whether inflation is becoming entrenched.
Markets will now focus on whether the BOJ uses its upcoming meeting to signal or deliver a further tightening step. A move that narrowed the interest rate gap with other major economies could help support the yen, easing one of the main sources of imported inflation. For now, the September figures suggest the softer headline reading has not changed the underlying picture of strong cost pressure.

China and North Korea yesterday officially opened their most significant land border crossing, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce.
Trucks festooned with the national flags of the neighbors drove across the long-delayed 3km New Yalu River Bridge, its towering pylons also decked in flags, linking the Chinese city of Dandong with North Korea.
Knots of spectators crowded a road on the Chinese side overlooking the cable-stayed bridge completed in 2014, but unused while North Korea left its approach roads and customs compound unfinished.
Photo: Reuters
Bilateral “relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter,” Chinese Premier Li Qiang (李強) said in a video address at the opening, the official Xinhua news agency reported.
The border crossing would “strongly promote” economic and trade cooperation, and further strengthen exchanges between their people, Li said.
It also offers an opportunity to improve border clearance procedures, boost connectivity and build cooperation in border areas, he said.
North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song also delivered a video address, Xinhua said, but North Korea’s state media were yet to report on the event.
The opening is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang after two summits between their leaders in the past year.
However, despite the potential economic boost from trade, analysts said North Korea remains cautious of greater dependence on China.
“The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade,” said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
The bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development efforts, Lim said.
China is by far Pyongyang’s largest trading partner, even after a series of UN sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers with the North over the latter’s missile and nuclear weapons development.
China and Russia, permanent members of the UN Security Council that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans.
Russia is accused by countries such as the US and South Korea of supplying sensitive military assistance to the North in return for Pyongyang’s help in fighting the war in Ukraine.
The delay in opening the bridge was a setback for Dandong, whose economy thrived in the early 21st century as the primary trade gateway to North Korea’s isolated economy.
Until now, most goods have crossed about 10km upstream, using an 83-year-old bridge with a rail track and a single-lane road. That remains the busiest of about 15 crossing points along the roughly 1,350km shared border.
Dandong residents welcomed the opening.
“It’s been more than a decade since they first said the bridge would open ... but coming here today and seeing it for myself makes me incredibly happy,” said a 50-year-old resident surnamed He.
“Once the bridge opens, this place will become much livelier, attracting more tourists,” said another Dandong resident, surnamed Xie.
The bridge opening was “effectively the first visible case” of adoption of agreements struck at a June summit of leaders, a South Korean Ministry of Unification official said.

articles.summary: North Korea is opening bridges to China and Russia, and only one is irreplaceable  Tomorrow's Affairs
articles.full_text:
Today, trucks bearing Chinese and North Korean flags crossed the new bridge over the Yalu River between China’s Dandong and North Korea’s Sinuiju.
Construction was completed in 2014, but the crossing then waited 12 years for roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side.
In a video address at the ceremony, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said that relations between the two countries had entered a new phase.
For Beijing, this marks the completion of an expensive investment, and for Kim Jong Un it marks the start of more regular supplies across the border on which his economy depends.
A little over a month ago, North Korea also opened a new road bridge to Russia.
The two links were created at a time when Beijing and Moscow are particularly important for the survival of the North Korean regime, but for completely different reasons.
China accounts for most reported foreign trade and has financed a major border crossing.
During the war in Ukraine, Russia has been procuring North Korean weapons, hiring soldiers and workers, and providing military aid that Pyongyang has been trying to secure for years.
Kim can now benefit more from relations with both powers, as both Beijing and Moscow need him.
Russian demand, however, is determined by the course of the war, and Chinese demand by the daily needs of the North Korean economy.
The new bridge is approximately 3,030 metres long, has four traffic lanes and is located about 13 kilometres south-west of the old Friendship Bridge.
China fully financed its construction, which began in 2009, at a cost of approximately 2.2 billion yuan, about $310 million.
The old crossing has a railway track and only one lane for vehicles, so trucks can pass only alternately.
The route between Dandong and Sinuiju carries more than 70 per cent of the two countries’ official trade.
The increased capacity is particularly important for transporting machinery, construction materials and industrial equipment.
Incomplete infrastructure on the North Korean side was an immediate obstacle to opening the bridge
Incomplete infrastructure on the North Korean side was an immediate obstacle to opening the bridge.
The delay also coincided with a cooling of relations after China backed UN Security Council sanctions over North Korea’s nuclear and missile tests in 2016 and 2017.
Kim’s visit to Beijing in September 2025 and Xi’s visit to Pyongyang in June this year accelerated completion of the works that the Chinese side had been awaiting since 2014.
The bridge thus represents a tangible outcome of diplomatic rapprochement.
A comparison with the previous period shows the potential for trade growth. According to Chinese customs data, bilateral trade was worth $2.73 billion in 2025, down from $6.86 billion in 2014.
Today’s volume is approximately 40 per cent of the earlier level. South Korea’s state agency Kotra, which uses its own foreign trade records, estimates that China accounted for 98.2 per cent of North Korea’s total reported trade last year.
Such concentration gives Beijing extraordinary influence over its neighbour’s supply and investment plans, independent of Moscow’s political role.
Kim’s value to Moscow increased as the war in Ukraine began to consume vast quantities of ammunition and manpower.
According to the first report of the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, published in May 2025, during 2024 Russian ships transported from North Korea up to nine million artillery shells and rockets for multiple-barrel rocket launchers, as well as at least 100 ballistic missiles.
The same report states that Pyongyang sent more than 11,000 soldiers to Russia at the end of 2024, and more than 3,000 at the beginning of 2025.
In return, Moscow provides Kim with military equipment and expertise that Pyongyang cannot obtain elsewhere because of sanctions.
According to the same report, Russia has delivered at least one Pantsir system to shoot down aircraft, missiles and drones, as well as electronic jamming equipment.
It has also supplied data on how North Korean ballistic missiles hit targets in Ukraine, which has helped to improve their guidance.
Russian instructors have been training North Korean soldiers in the use of artillery and drones, so Kim’s army is now gaining experience in a real war and its weapons are being tested on the battlefield.
Moscow is supplying Pyongyang with strategically important goods
The Russian export of petroleum products is particularly significant. A UN Security Council resolution limits North Korea’s annual supply of such products to 500,000 barrels.
Research by the Open Source Centre and the BBC, cited by the international team, identified 43 North Korean tanker arrivals at a Russian port between March and October 2024 and shipments estimated at more than one million barrels.
Moscow is therefore supplying Pyongyang with strategically important goods in quantities that, according to those findings, significantly exceed the permitted annual quota.
The Tumen River Bridge opened on 7 September in the far north-east of North Korea.
It connects the Russian settlement of Khasan in Primorsky Krai, south-west of Vladivostok, with North Korea’s Tumangang, at the point where the borders of Russia, China and North Korea meet.
Russia and North Korea share a border that is only 17 kilometres long, and until now it has been connected only by a railway bridge and air routes.
The new road bridge is about a kilometre long, has two lanes, and can accommodate up to 300 vehicles per day.
The Chinese bridge is much larger and serves a different purpose. It connects China’s Dandong, a port city at the confluence of the Yalu River and the Yellow Sea, with Sinuiju in north-western North Korea, about 200 kilometres from Pyongyang.
That route carries the largest share of North Korea’s trade with the rest of the world.
The Russian connection is more modest and supports cooperation that has developed during the war in Ukraine, primarily in the military industry and politics.
A September report by the same international team estimated that, at the end of 2025, between 20,000 and 70,000 North Korean citizens were working in China, and between 15,000 and 30,000 in Russia, where there had been about 8,000 a year earlier. In Russia, they are also employed in war-related industries.
The team alleges that North Korean workers were sent to Geran-2 drone factories in the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan.
More than 98 per cent of the visas that Russia issued to North Korean citizens in 2025 were student visas, and Russian regulations have been changed so that even with such a visa they may work for a salary.
The report describes the use of student visas for work in construction, manufacturing and agriculture.
It is estimated that over the last year the regime has earned between $450 million and $800 million from the work of its citizens abroad, taking 80 to 90 per cent of their earnings.
Behind that income are people working under strict supervision, often in extremely difficult conditions.
Beijing, which previously supported the imposition of sanctions, is now renewing economic ties with Pyongyang
According to the September report, Chinese firms’ employment of North Korean workers is also a violation of Security Council bans, as are Russia’s dealings with Pyongyang.
In March 2024, Russia vetoed the extension of the mandate of the UN expert group that monitored the implementation of sanctions against North Korea.
The bans themselves remained in force, and 11 countries later established a multilateral team to collect evidence of violations.
For Pyongyang, the Russian veto was an important diplomatic asset, as regular international supervision was weakened.
Thus, in addition to weapons and oil, Moscow made available its influence in the Security Council.
Beijing, which previously supported the imposition of sanctions, is now renewing economic ties with a neighbour whose military programme enjoys increasing backing from Russia.
At a military parade in Beijing on 3 September 2025, Kim stood alongside Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
China and Russia now share an interest in maintaining relations with Pyongyang and limiting American influence in Asia.
Kim exploits the fact that each of them has a different reason for continuing to work with him.
Xi’s visit to Pyongyang on 8–9 June was his first since 2019. Chinese and North Korean statements after the meeting omitted any reference to denuclearisation, as did China’s announcement of Kim’s visit to Beijing in 2025.
Beijing thereby emphasises political stability and cooperation, while North Korea’s nuclear arsenal remains off the published agenda for the meetings.
Xi also proposed increasing military exchanges, which was mentioned in the Chinese account but omitted from the North Korean account of the talks.
Such a relationship suits Kim, who receives trade concessions and political support without any public debate about relinquishing his most important deterrent.
At the same time, Beijing maintains influence over a neighbouring state whose destabilisation would threaten China’s border and security interests on the Korean Peninsula.
Moscow gains support for the war, while North Korea gains access to Russian military technology and additional revenue. T
heir interests currently align closely enough for the three governments to sustain close cooperation.
Over the next year, trade through Dandong, a Chinese city on the border with North Korea, is likely to grow, but because of sanctions and North Korea’s weak economy it will remain well below its 2014 level.
Military cooperation with Russia will greatly benefit Pyongyang as long as Moscow needs North Korean munitions and workers for its weapons factories during the war.
The 2024 partnership agreement will remain in place after the war, but once Russia needs fewer weapons and men, Kim will no longer be able to obtain from it what he receives today.

articles.summary: South Korea Plans 22% Crypto Tax Guidelines for November  Serrari Group
articles.full_text:
Share
South Korea’s National Tax Service (NTS) plans to publish detailed cryptocurrency tax guidelines in November 2026, ahead of a scheduled tax regime taking effect on 1 January 2027. The proposed rules impose a combined 22% tax on qualifying annual digital-asset gains exceeding 2.5 million won. Officials are still clarifying the treatment of staking, airdrops, hard forks and decentralised finance transactions, while exchanges prepare their reporting systems.
Key Overview
- Guidelines: Expected in November 2026.
- Tax rate: 22%, comprising national and local income taxes.
- Annual deduction: 2.5 million South Korean won.
- Implementation date: 1 January 2027.
- First tax returns: Expected in May 2028 for income earned during 2027.
- Outstanding issues: Treatment of certain crypto transactions and exchange reporting readiness.
South Korea Prepares Detailed Crypto Tax Rules
South Korea is preparing to introduce detailed cryptocurrency taxation guidance as the government moves towards implementing its long-delayed digital-asset tax regime. The National Tax Service expects to release its crypto tax guidelines in November, giving investors and exchanges more clarity before the planned January 2027 start.
The announcement followed a parliamentary audit on 13 October 2026, during which NTS Commissioner Lim Gwang-hyeon discussed preparations with lawmakers. The tax authority is working with domestic cryptocurrency exchanges and the Ministry of Finance and Economy to develop the necessary procedures.
The guidelines are expected to address practical questions about calculating taxable income, recording transactions and classifying different forms of digital-asset earnings. These details will be important for investors who trade through multiple platforms or receive cryptocurrency through activities other than buying and selling.
The planned release comes after several postponements of the tax regime, which was originally scheduled to begin in 2022. Authorities are now preparing for implementation under the existing legal timetable, although further political debate remains possible.
Qualifying Crypto Gains Face a 22% Tax
Under the current framework, qualifying income from transferring or lending digital assets will be subject to a combined 22% tax when the regime begins on 1 January 2027.
The rate consists of a 20% national income tax and an additional 2% local income tax. The levy applies to qualifying annual gains exceeding the basic deduction of 2.5 million won.
Taxable income is calculated after accounting for eligible acquisition costs and transaction expenses. Annual gains and losses are combined before the basic deduction is applied, with the remaining qualifying amount taxed under the applicable rules.
The 22% crypto tax is intended to bring qualifying digital-asset income within the country’s tax framework. However, the rules distinguish taxable income from the full value of an investor’s cryptocurrency holdings: the levy concerns qualifying gains, not simply the amount of cryptocurrency owned.
Investors who acquired assets before the tax takes effect may also need to consider special rules for determining acquisition value. Keeping records of purchase prices, transaction costs and transfers could therefore be important when calculating future tax liabilities.
Staking, Airdrops and DeFi Remain Under Review
One of the main challenges is determining how the tax rules will apply to cryptocurrency activities beyond conventional trading.
Officials are reviewing the treatment of staking rewards, airdrops, hard forks and decentralised finance (DeFi) transactions. These activities can generate digital assets through different mechanisms, making it necessary to establish when income arises and how it should be valued.
Airdrops and hard forks may be taxable when their economic characteristics meet the relevant legal requirements. The treatment of staking and some DeFi activities still requires further clarification and coordination between the tax authority and the finance ministry.
The upcoming guidance is expected to help investors and exchanges understand how such transactions should be recorded and reported. Until the standards are formally published, some details remain unresolved.

Exchanges Face Reporting and Enforcement Challenges
South Korea’s tax authority is also working to ensure cryptocurrency exchanges can provide the information needed to calculate taxable gains.
During the parliamentary audit, lawmakers questioned whether exchanges would have sufficiently consistent transaction records and reporting systems in place before the deadline. The NTS has been consulting domestic platforms to prepare for implementation.
Transactions conducted through overseas exchanges and private wallets present additional challenges. Although qualifying income may fall within the tax framework regardless of where the assets are held, authorities can face difficulties obtaining complete records of transactions that occur outside domestic platforms.
South Korea expects international information-sharing arrangements, including the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, to improve access to overseas transaction data. However, these systems may not capture every transaction, particularly transfers between privately controlled wallets.
The reporting challenge means that publishing tax rules is only one part of implementation. Authorities must also establish practical systems for collecting, analysing and verifying the information required to enforce the regime.
First Returns Expected in May 2028
If the existing timetable remains unchanged, the tax regime will begin on January 1, 2027, with the first tax returns covering qualifying income earned during that year expected in May 2028.
The time between the guideline release and implementation will be important for exchanges updating their reporting infrastructure and for investors preparing records.
The policy has faced repeated delays amid concerns about compliance costs, administrative readiness and whether cryptocurrency income would be treated consistently with other investments. Some lawmakers continue to call for further postponement or changes to the framework, but no new delay has been confirmed.
Outlook
South Korea’s planned November guidance will be an important step towards implementing its cryptocurrency tax regime. The combined 22% rate and 2.5 million won annual deduction provide the broad framework, but the treatment of complex transactions and the availability of reliable reporting data remain significant issues.
Investors and exchanges will be watching for clear rules on taxable income, acquisition costs, staking and other digital-asset activities. The outcome will help determine how smoothly the regime can begin in January 2027 and how effectively authorities can verify reported gains.

articles.title: EU Moves to Lift China Sanctions to Save German Chipmaking Materials Supplier - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: EU Moves to Lift China Sanctions to Save German Chipmaking Materials Supplier  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
BEIJING — The European Union is pushing to lift sanctions on a Chinese company in order to rescue a German semiconductor parts maker pushed to the brink of collapse by China's rare earth restrictions.
At high-level trade talks held in Beijing on the 8th and 9th of this month, the EU and China discussed lifting trade restrictions imposed on a Chinese company suspected of supporting Russia's war in exchange for China lifting sanctions on Germany's Schindelhauser Materials, Bloomberg reported on the 14th. Schindelhauser is a small and midsize company specializing in precision semiconductor manufacturing and advanced coatings, and it supplies parts to ASML, the world's largest maker of semiconductor lithography equipment.
The EU had earlier sanctioned the Chinese company on the grounds that it supplied key components used in weapons production to Russia. China retaliated in July by adding 14 European companies, including Schindelhauser, to its export control list. Schindelhauser depends entirely on supplies of Chinese rare earths and critical minerals and is said to face the risk of shutting down within months if the Chinese sanctions remain in place.
Analysts say the targeting of a little-known German small business shows how meticulously China is moving to weaponize its resources. Over the past year and a half, China has used licensing requirements for critical minerals and rare earths to collect wide-ranging information on global supply chains. It requires foreign companies to submit detailed materials, including information on end customers, how Chinese raw materials are used and photographs of final products. Observers say this allowed China to identify weak links in the supply chain of Europe's semiconductor industry and strike them with precision.
Bloomberg noted that German companies are handing over trade secrets to China while the German government cannot obtain even a comparable level of information, adding that the more serious problem is that Berlin has yet to devise a strategy to address this gap in economic intelligence-gathering capability.

articles.full_text:
South Korea's benchmark stock market suffered a sharp sell-off on Thursday, October 15, as mounting concerns over US inflation and the sustainability of artificial intelligence investments triggered heavy selling in semiconductor and other technology-linked shares. The KOSPI plunged 7.57% to close at 5,554.22, marking its seventh consecutive session of losses and taking the index to a six-month low.
South Korea Stock Market Crash: KOSPI Plunges 7.57% to 6-Month Low
The sell-off placed South Korea's technology-heavy equity market at the centre of a broader global reassessment of AI-linked stocks. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, two of the country's largest listed companies and major suppliers to the global semiconductor industry, led the decline.
Their losses came as Wall Street's technology shares weakened following stronger-than-expected US inflation data, renewing fears that interest rates could remain elevated and increase the pressure on high-growth companies.
KOSPI Crash: Why Did South Korea's Stock Market Trigger a Sidecar?
The Korea Exchange activated a sell-side "sidecar" after a steep drop in index futures crossed the market's volatility threshold. The mechanism temporarily suspends programme sell orders for five minutes, giving trading conditions an opportunity to stabilise during an abrupt market move. It does not shut down the entire stock market, but is intended to slow automated selling when price movements become unusually sharp.
As technology stocks fell, pressure spread across major index constituents, amplifying the benchmark's decline. The KOSPI's seventh straight session of losses also indicated that Thursday's rout was part of a broader deterioration in investor sentiment, rather than an isolated intraday correction.
Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix Shares Lead the Sell-Off
South Korea's semiconductor heavyweights bore the brunt of the selling. Samsung Electronics shares fell 9.05%, while SK Hynix dropped 11.06%, according to the reported market figures. Given their importance to the benchmark, steep declines in both companies exerted significant pressure on the wider KOSPI.
The two companies are central to the global memory-chip supply chain, but investors are increasingly weighing the growth opportunity presented by AI against the cost and returns of the infrastructure supporting it. Samsung is a major memory-chip manufacturer, while SK Hynix is a key supplier of high-bandwidth memory used in advanced AI computing systems.
US Inflation Revives Interest-Rate Fears
The immediate global trigger was the latest US inflation reading. Consumer prices rose 3.7% year-on-year in September, while the monthly increase was 0.6%, adding to concerns that inflationary pressure remains persistent. The data weakened hopes of a quick easing in monetary policy and fuelled expectations that the US Federal Reserve may have to maintain restrictive rates for longer.
That prospect can weigh heavily on technology and growth stocks. When interest rates are high, the future earnings of companies tend to be valued less generously, while borrowing to fund large investment programs becomes more expensive. The pressure is particularly relevant to the AI sector, where businesses are committing substantial resources to data centres, computing capacity and advanced chips in anticipation of future demand.

articles.title: South Korea's KOSPI Plunges 8%, Halting Trading as AI Rout Deepens - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: South Korea's KOSPI Plunges 8%, Halting Trading as AI Rout Deepens  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
South Korean stocks suffered their sharpest single-day rout in months on Thursday, with the benchmark KOSPI tumbling 8% and triggering a marketwide circuit breaker as a global selloff in technology and semiconductor shares intensified.
The Korea Exchange halted trading on the main KOSPI board at 12:38 p.m. local time after the index remained at least 8% below its previous close for one minute. The halt, which lasted 20 minutes, marked the 10th circuit breaker this year and the 16th since the mechanism was introduced. At the time of the suspension, the KOSPI stood at 5,528.05, down 480.76 points, its lowest level since July 29. Ten of those 16 halts have come this year alone, against just six in the quarter-century from 2000 through 2024; the previous one came on July 29, capping the first back-to-back trading halt across both Korean markets, after the KOSPI plunged 10.84% on July 28 and fell a further 5.98% the next day.
The benchmark later recovered part of its losses, trading at 5,589.19, down 6.98%, as of early afternoon. The tech-heavy KOSDAQ also triggered a circuit breaker earlier, at 12:23 p.m., when it was 8.01% lower at 757.88.
Chip Giants Lead the Decline
Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK Hynix (000660.KS), the two dominant forces in the Korean equity market, bore the brunt of the selling. Samsung fell as much as 9.7% to 211,250 won, while SK Hynix plunged 11.35% to 1.275 million won. The two companies account for nearly half of the KOSPI's market capitalization, meaning their losses disproportionately dragged down the broader index.
The selloff followed a 4.3% drop in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index overnight, extending its losing streak to six consecutive sessions. US chipmakers faced heavy pressure after CoreWeave, an AI cloud computing company, saw its shares plummet 15.46% on concerns about its debt-funded expansion strategy. Some of the company's bonds were trading at distressed levels, with yields exceeding 15%, raising questions about whether its business model of borrowing to build data centers and repaying debt through customer usage fees is sustainable. Oracle, another company at the center of the AI infrastructure buildout, fell about 9% on Wednesday, underscoring how quickly scrutiny has shifted from AI demand to AI finance.
Inflation Data Fuels Rate Fears
The rout was amplified by hotter-than-expected US inflation data released on Wednesday. The September consumer price index rose 3.7% year over year, above the 3.6% consensus forecast. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, climbed 2.6%, also exceeding the 2.5% estimate. The data strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve may keep interest rates elevated or even raise them further, undermining the valuation case for richly priced technology stocks.
"The market is reacting more sensitively to whether AI funding is sustainable and whether massive infrastructure investment will translate into actual revenue, rather than to the growth in AI service sales itself," said Seo Sang-young, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities.
Foreign investors were the primary sellers, dumping a net 3.62 trillion won (approximately $2.6 billion) of KOSPI shares on Thursday. Retail and institutional investors absorbed the supply with net purchases of 1.29 trillion won and 1.69 trillion won respectively, but could not stem the decline. Foreign investors have now been net sellers for eight consecutive sessions.
AI Investment Model Under Scrutiny
Beyond the immediate inflation shock, investors are reassessing the fundamental economics of the AI infrastructure boom. The CoreWeave episode has crystallized concerns that the massive capital expenditures required to build data centers and acquire chips may not generate sufficient returns to justify the borrowing costs.
The worries now extend well beyond a single borrower. On Wednesday, Gartner estimated that more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to impairment by the end of 2030 if providers maintain their current pace of capital spending, and projected that more than 80% of neocloud providers — the smaller, AI-focused data center operators of which CoreWeave is the best-known — will cease independent operations by 2030. The research firm calculated that data center owners would need to generate a cumulative $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030 to cover announced capital spending, financing costs and a 12% return on invested capital.
"Concerns over the sustainability of AI investment beyond the next 12 months have prompted the market to revert to valuing semiconductor stocks as commodity-driven cyclicals," wrote Mingyu Kim, an analyst at KB Securities, in a note to clients.
flowchart TD
    CPI[US September CPI tops forecasts] --> RATES[Fed easing bets fade]
    RATES --> VAL[Richly valued tech and chip shares under pressure]
    CW[CoreWeave bonds yield near 15 percent] --> FUND[Doubts over AI infrastructure financing]
    RISK[3.5 trillion dollars of AI capex seen at risk] --> FUND
    FUND --> DEMAND[Memory demand outlook questioned]
    VAL --> DEMAND
    DEMAND --> KR[Samsung and SK Hynix plunge]
    KR --> IDX[KOSPI down 8 percent, circuit breaker tripped]
    IDX --> ASIA[Nikkei 225 and Taiex follow]
Even strong earnings have failed to reassure investors. Samsung Electronics forecast a nearly ninefold increase in third-quarter operating profit last week, yet its shares have since lost almost a fifth of their value. ASML Holding (ASML) also reported solid results and said equipment demand is likely to exceed supply through 2028, with customers already discussing capacity for 2029 and 2030, but the news did little to stem the selling.
The KOSPI's decline extends a brutal reversal for a market that was among the world's best performers in the first half of 2026. The index more than doubled before peaking at a record 9,385.59 on June 19. It has since fallen roughly 41% from that high, transforming South Korea from the top-performing major market in the first half to the worst performer in the second.
Competitive Threats From China
Adding to the pressure on Korean chipmakers is the competitive threat from China. ChangXin Memory Technologies, China's largest DRAM manufacturer, announced plans to release next-generation server memory products by the end of the year. The new products are expected to reduce the cell area for data storage by about 33%, potentially narrowing the technological gap with established players like Samsung and SK Hynix.
"Unlike advanced foundries such as TSMC, domestic semiconductor companies are highly sensitive to changes in memory prices and supply, causing their profits to react sharply," said Yoon Chang-yong, head of Shinhan Securities Research Center. "The entry of Chinese companies into the mix and the expansion of supply will inevitably place a greater burden on domestic semiconductor stocks."
The competitive concern is not merely hypothetical. The memory chip industry has historically been highly cyclical, with periods of shortage and price increases followed by supply expansion and oversupply. Investors who had been willing to pay premium valuations for AI-related growth are now questioning whether those multiples are justified when the competitive landscape is shifting.
Market Structure Amplifies the Decline
The concentration of the Korean market in a handful of semiconductor names has made it particularly vulnerable to the AI trade reversal. Beyond Samsung and SK Hynix, other Korean chip-related stocks suffered steep losses: LG Innotek fell 8.1%, Seoul Semiconductor dropped 7.7%, and Samsung SDI declined 6.8%. In the broader KOSPI, Sanil Electric fell 16.9%, Samsung Electro-Mechanics lost 16.8%, and Hansol Technics was down 15.2%.
At the close, the damage across the AI supply chain was broad:

The selloff reached beyond chipmakers into the equipment and power-infrastructure suppliers that had ranked among the market's biggest AI winners.
Mixo Das, head of Korea equity strategy at JP Morgan in Hong Kong, noted that share buybacks by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which had supported the market since August, are winding down. "The market is struggling to find new buyers," he said, adding that this process would likely continue in the coming weeks. He maintained his forecast that AI-related stocks would rise further over a 6-12 month horizon.
The recovery that briefly lifted the index in the afternoon did not hold. The KOSPI closed at 5,554.22, down 7.57% — its lowest close since July 30 — and the KOSDAQ finished 7.65% lower at 760.82. Defensive shares drew buyers as investors rotated out of AI-linked names: Samsung Biologics rose 5.5%, Yuhan gained 5.09% and KT&G added 3.96%.
Regional Contagion
The Korean selloff was part of a broader regional decline. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell more than 4% to around 65,000, with SoftBank Group (9984.T) down 7.9% and semiconductor equipment makers Advantest (6857.T) and Tokyo Electron (8035.T) falling 6.9% and 5.4% respectively. The index finished the day 4.8% lower at 64,489.06. Taiwan's Taiex lost 3.4%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng shed 1%, the Shanghai Composite fell 1.4% and Australia's ASX 200 edged 0.1% lower.

A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours.
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea and is set to become the main land route for trade between the two.
Its launch, initially slated for 2014, was indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities as relations with Beijing turned frosty.
The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.
It is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".
Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.
A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC.
"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds.
"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."
Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.
But the alliance is not without tension.
Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan.
China's attitude has shifted more recently.
"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC.
Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war.
At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops.
Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people to cross every day.
So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties.
Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

articles.title: Samsung, SK hynix escalate Korea AI chip race with HBM4E and new memory - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Samsung, SK hynix escalate Korea AI chip race with HBM4E and new memory - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix unveiled the seventh-generation high-bandwidth memory (HBM), "HBM4E," side by side, kicking off a race in next-generation artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor technology. The two companies not only boosted the performance of existing HBM but also showcased new technologies that change memory placement architecture and data storage methods. As AI models grow larger, reducing bottlenecks in data movement between compute units and memory has emerged as a key task for the chip industry.
According to the chip industry on the 15th, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix unveiled HBM4E and other next-generation memory technologies at the 28th Semiconductor Exhibition (SEDEX 2026), which opened on the 14th at COEX in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. About 300 corporations in semiconductor design and manufacturing, and materials, parts, and equipment took part in the event, which runs through the 16th.
The flagship product both companies put forward is HBM4E. HBM is memory that stacks multiple DRAM dies vertically to increase data processing speed and is used in AI accelerators such as Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs). As data needed for training and inference of AI models surges, technologies that boost HBM's bandwidth, capacity, and power efficiency are becoming increasingly important.
Samsung Electronics' HBM4E combines 10-nanometer-class sixth-generation (1c) DRAM with a base die built on a 4-nanometer foundry process. Per-pin data transfer speed ranges from 14 Gbps up to 16 Gbps, more than 20% higher than HBM4, the previous generation. Maximum memory bandwidth reaches 3.6 TB per second.
The 12-high stack product has a capacity of 48 GB, up more than 30% from its predecessor. Samsung Electronics plans to expand the lineup with 8-high 32 GB and 16-high 64 GB products. In May, it supplied samples of the 12-high HBM4E to customers and is pushing for mass production in line with customer schedules.
SK hynix also introduced HBM4E with data transfer speeds up to 16 Gbps. It features more than a 20% improvement in energy efficiency over existing HBM4. SK hynix supplied 12-high HBM4E samples to major customers in June and is conducting performance verification.
◇ Samsung stacks memory on GPUs; SK develops new memory between HBM and SSDs
Another technology that drew attention at the exhibition was Samsung Electronics' "zHBM" and SK hynix's "HBF (high-bandwidth flash)." Both aim to reduce memory bottlenecks in AI systems, but they take different approaches.
Samsung Electronics unveiled a model of zHBM, a three-dimensional (3D) memory architecture that vertically stacks HBM on top of the compute unit, rather than placing it next to the GPU. By shortening the physical distance between the compute unit and memory, it reduces the time and power required for data movement.
Samsung Electronics also exhibited "LPDDR-PIM (processing in memory)," which handles some computation inside memory. The technology improves power efficiency by reducing the number of times data is moved to the compute unit. It also introduced "zNAND-O," a 3D NAND solution usable in Edge AI devices.
SK hynix presented HBF, which combines HBM's fast data processing with NAND flash's large-capacity storage, as a next-generation technology. HBF aims to offer high bandwidth while storing far more data than existing HBM.
Today's AI servers build a memory and storage hierarchy with HBM, conventional DRAM, and solid-state drives (SSDs). SK hynix plans to insert HBF between them to reduce data processing burdens that arise during inference in large-scale AI models. The company said it expects HBF to offer about 10 times the capacity of existing HBM.
Ahn Hyeon, head of development at SK hynix, said in a keynote speech at the Semiconductor Exhibition on the 14th that the performance scale of AI infrastructure will be about 20 times larger in 2030 than this year. Ahn emphasized that, beyond conventional HBM, new memory technologies such as custom HBM, 3D-stacked DRAM, and HBF are needed to improve performance and efficiency across AI systems.
◇ HBM competition expands to foundry and packaging capabilities
In the next-generation HBM market, not only memory manufacturing technology but also logic chip design and advanced packaging capabilities are becoming important. That is because demand is expected to rise for custom products that design HBM base dies to match customers' AI accelerator architectures.
Samsung Electronics also unveiled a 4-nanometer base die for HBM4E, a 2-nanometer Gate-All-Around (GAA) wafer, and advanced packaging technologies "2.3D Cube-E" and "3D Cube-H." The strategy is to leverage its business structure spanning memory, foundry, system semiconductors, and packaging to target the next-generation AI Semiconductor market.
SK hynix showcased high-performance server DRAM alongside HBM4E, including 256 GB 3DS RDIMM and 128 GB MRDIMM. It also displayed an HBM wafer bearing the signature of Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive officer (CEO), and the company's next-generation AI platform, the "Vera Rubin" Superchip, highlighting its collaboration with customers.
Industry watchers say the AI Semiconductor race is expanding from boosting HBM's data transfer speed and capacity to innovating the memory architecture itself. As AI models scale up and inference services spread, technologies that reduce not only memory bandwidth constraints but also storage capacity limits, power consumption, and systemwide data movement expense are becoming more important.
However, since zHBM and HBF remain at the concept and development stages of next-generation technologies, the timing of commercialization and whether customers adopt them will likely determine their competitiveness.

articles.title: South Korean opposition attacks President Lee over golf outing during Daegu supermarket collapse - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: South Korean opposition attacks President Lee over golf outing during Daegu supermarket collapse  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
South Korea's main opposition party has launched a fierce attack against President Lee Jae Myung, questioning his judgment and crisis management capabilities after he was photographed playing golf while a major infrastructure disaster unfolded in the city of Daegu. The controversy centres on a partial ceiling collapse at a large supermarket in Daegu on Saturday morning, an incident that left at least 38 people injured and required a massive emergency response.
The People Power Party (PPP) condemned the President's weekend schedule, arguing that his presence at the Taereung Country Club in northern Seoul was highly inappropriate given the scale of the emergency. PPP leader Jang Dong-hyeok publicly challenged the administration, asking whether a single line of instruction given from a golf course constitutes the right attitude for a head of state responsible for the lives of citizens. He further questioned the logistical feasibility of receiving real-time situation reports and issuing effective emergency directives while actively engaged in a leisure sport.
The opposition's criticism intensified when PPP chief spokesperson Park Sung-hoon released a commentary accusing President Lee of enjoying an "imperial" round of golf. In South Korean political discourse, the term "imperial" is frequently used to describe outings that are exceptionally leisurely, prolonged, and detached from the daily struggles of ordinary citizens, contrasting sharply with the rushed schedules of the general public. The PPP argued that the presidential office attempted to deceive the public by framing the outing as an extension of official duties.
In defence of the President, the ruling Democratic Party (DP) and officials from Cheong Wa Dae maintained that Lee Jae Myung fulfilled his constitutional duties despite his location. The presidential office released a statement confirming that immediately upon receiving reports of the Daegu supermarket collapse, the President issued an order from the golf course mandating a thorough and exhaustive rescue operation. DP spokesperson Cho Gye-won added that the outing was partly preparatory, suggesting it was intended to ready the President for potential "golf diplomacy" with United States President Donald Trump.
The decision to publicly announce the President's private schedule was an unusual move by the presidential office, reportedly triggered by threats from PPP lawmaker Joo Jin-woo to hold a press conference exposing Lee's location during the disaster. By pre-emptively confirming his visit to the country club with his family, the administration sought to control the narrative and demonstrate transparency, though it inadvertently provided the opposition with the exact timeline needed to mount their criticism.
The Daegu incident itself involved the sudden collapse of a section of ceiling in a busy supermarket, trapping shoppers and staff under debris. Emergency services worked through the weekend to extract the injured and secure the structure, with the final tally of injuries reaching 38. The severity of the incident naturally drew national attention, making the President's absence from the crisis command centre a highly visible point of political vulnerability.
Political analysts in Seoul note that the "golf controversy" is a recurring trope in South Korean politics, where leaders are frequently judged on their optics during national tragedies. Previous administrations have faced severe backlash for perceived indifference or poor timing of leisure activities during crises, and the current opposition is leveraging this historical sensitivity to damage President Lee's approval ratings. The debate highlights the intense scrutiny placed on the executive branch in South Korea, where the boundary between private rest and public duty is constantly contested.
As the rescue and cleanup operations in Daegu continue, the political fallout shows no signs of abating. The ruling party maintains that the President's directives were executed flawlessly by the relevant ministries, while the opposition insists that true leadership requires physical presence and undivided attention during moments of national distress. The incident has undoubtedly set a combative tone for the upcoming parliamentary sessions, with the PPP signalling its intent to use the controversy to scrutinise the administration's broader emergency preparedness.
